utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Let the witness make the declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: You may sit. And before you begin, I think I should explain why we're starting at 9.30, or 9.31. The witness who was testifying yesterday and who would normally be testifying today is ill and is unable to testify. That meant that the next witness was called up. That, however, created some difficulties for the Prosecution because the Prosecutor who was to take this witness was not -- was not available at that time. We find that to be quite understandable and therefore we agreed to start at 9.30. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Thank you for that, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Tapuskovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours. Thank you. We will begin the examination-in-chief of the next witness, but before I put any questions --

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: I am not getting the translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I think it has just started.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, before I ask you anything, please pay attention to the monitor before you, and when the text stops moving, only then begin answering my questions, as you see happening now. Can you tell Their Honours your full name.

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG TRAPARA
utterances.text: My name is Predrag Trapara.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Please look at the text on the monitor and wait for it to stop before answering, always. You were born on the 20th of January, 1964.

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG TRAPARA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: You were born in Sarajevo, in the municipality called Centar.

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG TRAPARA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: You completed primary school at Vrace and secondary building construction school, architecture, in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG TRAPARA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And you performed your civic duty in the JNA in 1983.

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG TRAPARA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Until the beginning of the conflict, you were employed as a postman in post office number 2 in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG TRAPARA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: All your life you lived in Lukavica, where you were born, and you still reside there today.

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG TRAPARA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us approximately when you joined the army of Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG TRAPARA
utterances.text: On the 10th of April, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell Their Honours what brigade you were a member of?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG TRAPARA
utterances.text: I was in the 1st Sarajevo Mechanised Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell Their Honours who the commander of the brigade was?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG TRAPARA
utterances.text: The commander of the brigade was Colonel Veljko Stojanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Who was the battalion commander of your battalion?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG TRAPARA
utterances.text: In the 2nd Infantry Battalion, the first battalion commander was Mr. Brane Pakalovic, who was wounded by a shell in Dobrinska Street.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And then?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG TRAPARA
utterances.text: After him it was the late Mr. Radomir Stojanovic, who was killed by a sniper near the police academy at Vrace.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And then?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG TRAPARA
utterances.text: And the third commander was Aleksandar Petrovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, may we go very briefly into private session. I have not asked for any protective measures for this witness, but in view of the fact that he does not wish to imperil the security of anybody else or himself, I would like him to mention some names in private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. Private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Can you -- can you now tell us what happened next?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG TRAPARA
utterances.text: When the policemen got out of the car, they only asked, Who is the driver of this truck? The driver reported to them and said, I am.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG TRAPARA
utterances.text: They didn't question anybody else. A policeman got on the truck with him and they drove off towards Vrace.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you say what you found out later on? Did you know what the cargo consisted of and what happened to you and to all those who had any connections with this? But don't mention any names now.

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG TRAPARA
utterances.text: Up to the house where we parked the truck, I didn't know what was in the truck. When the truck stopped, then they told me what was in it. After that, on the following day, my cousin and I continued doing our work in post office number 2 in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, but you didn't give us the most important piece of information. What was in the truck, and what happened? You say the police stopped that, so what happened next?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG TRAPARA
utterances.text: Yes. The police stopped the truck, as I said, and they went off towards Vrace. Later on --

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Please, Mr. Trapara, I'm asking you what was in the truck, what happened to you and what happened to the other people.

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG TRAPARA
utterances.text: The truck contained weapons. What kind of weapons and how many, I didn't know. Until the point in time when I was brought in to the military court in the Viktor Bubanj prison in Sarajevo, seven days after that event, and we had been working at our regular jobs for seven days.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Please explain to Their Honours. Were there any proceedings?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG TRAPARA
utterances.text: Yes, yes. I was brought in and I spent 29 days in the Viktor Bubanj prison, after which I was released. And I continued working at my job until the 10th of April, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: So this was --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Proceed, Mr. Tapuskovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: So this was sometime in September.

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG TRAPARA
utterances.text: Just before the end of October and then until the end of November, that's the time I spent in the Viktor Bubanj prison.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: That was in 1991. What police was that?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG TRAPARA
utterances.text: It was the police of the Socialist Federative Republic of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And whose military court were you tried before?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG TRAPARA
utterances.text: The military court of the Yugoslav People's Army, JNA.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: What happened to the weapons?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG TRAPARA
utterances.text: They were taken over by the JNA, the Yugoslav People's Army.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And until the beginning of the conflict, you didn't have any weapons?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG TRAPARA
utterances.text: No. It never occurred to me to get a weapon before the conflict began.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Mr. Tapuskovic, I'm not quite certain about the reason why the witness was arrested and apparently prosecuted. What were the charges raised against him?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, there were proceedings against a group, as he explained, against a group of persons which gained in an illegal manner weapons. And I'm not going to go into the reasons that the witness talked about. The police of the Socialist Federative Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, or, rather, the federal or that state of the former Yugoslavia, took measures and arrested the people who acquired the weapons illegally, after which proceedings were conducted because they possessed illegally acquired weapons. And because of that he spent about a month in prison. The weapons were seized via the police and the proceedings were held before the military tribunal in Sarajevo. This was in the autumn of 1994. No, no, actually 1991. And then after that he continued to work as a postman in the post office until the relevant events. There is a document about this. I knew about this from before and I believed that the witness needed to say something to you about that before moving to the rest of the testimony that relates to the indictment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you. I just did not hear the witness tell us this. But I think you should move on because this may not be strictly relevant to the case. So let's move up to the time of the indictment.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have a different view, and I will speak one day about why this is relevant. But I do accept your ruling at this point and we will move on to the relevant period. Following the decision regarding the adjudicated facts, I hope that we will no longer be in a situation when we cannot deal with the period of time from 1992 up until the end of the war anymore, and in that respect the Defence has to -- is, to a major degree, damaged. We will deal a little bit with that time period and the time period encompassing these things that the witness talked about that have to do with the things that preceded the conflict, the Green Berets, and all of that. All of that is important. To date, the Defence was not in a position to deal with things related to the adjudicated facts which we can actually dispute each one, except for maybe a single one. However, we will continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, what was your position in that brigade?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG TRAPARA
utterances.text: I was a company commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: I would like to ask you this first: You were born and you lived in Sarajevo. Can you say anything about what Sarajevo is for you?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG TRAPARA
utterances.text: Sarajevo comprises ten municipalities: Stari Grad, Centar, Novo Sarajevo, Novi Grad, Ilidza, Vogosca, Hadzici, Ilijas, Pale, and Trnovo.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. It's good that you remembered to mention each one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I was conferring with my colleague, Mr. Tapuskovic, because it seems to me that the pertinent question is not what, in the witness's view, is Sarajevo but what is the relevant geographical area for the purposes of this case, for the purposes of the indictment. The two things may not be the same.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I know. I don't think that this deserves -- I wouldn't want to say that. What I wanted to hear from him was -- well, my question was, actually, but I cannot run. I think it's necessary for the witness to first state with Sarajevo is, and now if he can - actually, that was going to be my next question - to say what the characteristics are.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: I'm not even going to ask you in a different way, other than what is characteristic about those areas that you spoke about for you, as someone who was born there. In the geographical sense, what is characteristic?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG TRAPARA
utterances.text: Compared to other towns, what is characteristic of Sarajevo is a large number of hills and elevations which I -- where I played as a child and I toured most of them as a child all around. As a child, I was a member of the Scouts organisation and I know most of those elevations very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And now can you mention the elevations that are so characteristic for the town of Sarajevo that had the municipalities that you mentioned?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG TRAPARA
utterances.text: First, I would start with the Mojmilo hill, which is just above my house where I was born, where I have land and had been living there, or our family had been living there for centuries. Stup hill, Sokolje, Zuc, Hum, Grdonj. And then looking from the southwest side, and I spent a lot of time on the mountain of Trebevic, then Vidakovic, Bistrik, Kula, Colina Kapa, Golo Brdo, and Zlatiste.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And was there anything all the way to the east, if you recall?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG TRAPARA
utterances.text: Yes. There was Hresa. Perhaps I forgot that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: You were a member of the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps. I'm going to ask you directly if you know when General Dragomir Milosevic became the commander of the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG TRAPARA
utterances.text: General Dragomir Milosevic became commander of the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps in August 1994.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And now, since you've already said that in April 1992 you joined the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps as a soldier and up until the time that Dragomir Milosevic became commander, how much time passed before he actually came?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG TRAPARA
utterances.text: Two years and four months, approximately.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Let me ask you: When he assumed the post of Sarajevo-Romanija Corps commander, can you please tell me, these elevations that you mentioned, who had control over them? Was it the army of Republika Srpska or the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG TRAPARA
utterances.text: Well, let me go in the same order that I mentioned them. First, Mojmilo. Along its entire length was under the control of the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina. Its dominant elevation was at some 680 metres. Stup hill was also under the control of the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina. Sokolje hill was also under the control of the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina. Zuc hill was also under the control of the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina. Hum also was under the control of the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina. Grdonj was also under the control of the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina. Hresa was under the control of the army of Republika Srpska. And then in the southwestern area, Mount Trebevic, where Vidikovac was, was under the control of the army of Republika Srpska. Colina Kapa was under the control of the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina. Bistrik, Kula, was under the control of the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina. Debelo Brdo was under the control of the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina. Zlatiste was under the control of the army of Republika Srpska, partially.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: May I ask you, Witness, when you say that a particular hill was under the control of the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina, does that mean that the army of Republika Srpska was not present at all on that hill, did not occupy any part of that hill, or do you mean that the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina occupied a dominant portion of the hill and the army of Republika Srpska did not? In other words, just explain what you mean by "under the control of the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When I say "under the control," what I mean was what you said second. The dominant elevations at those hills were under the control of the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina, specifically Mojmilo hill. All dominant elevations at Mojmilo hill were held by the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina. In the slope - the terrain is at a slope - in the middle of that slope were the forces of the army of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And now that we're talking about this, perhaps you can just show the Judges, and we can go as quickly as possible through that, since you said that the army of Republika Srpska was on the slopes of Mojmilo, you can indicate where you were with your company, where your positions were.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we please show the witness map 65 ter number 2872. Can we show this southern section of the map. Can we zoom in on that section, please. Yes, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, can you please indicate first where your house was? Are you able to see it here?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG TRAPARA
utterances.text: Just one moment, please. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Can you please mark that spot with the letter K.

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG TRAPARA
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And now can you please draw the line of separation, precisely the place where you were, you and your company.

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG TRAPARA
utterances.text: This is the area of responsibility of my company, approximately.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And where did this line emerge?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG TRAPARA
utterances.text: It went all along Mojmilo, below Mojmilo, to Vrace, where it reached the hill. At the other end it went beneath Mojmilo and then this way, where the line of separation went through Dobrinja IV. This here was the area of responsibility of my company.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Can you please indicate with a blue line the area of responsibility of your company. Just one moment, please.

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG TRAPARA
utterances.text: With a blue line.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, now you have a different colour, so now show where your company was.

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG TRAPARA
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Can you please mark where the Mojmilo ridge was? Can you mark Mojmilo?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG TRAPARA
utterances.text: Bogusevica was here and the ridge, Greben was right here.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Just one moment.

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG TRAPARA
utterances.text: This is the peak.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Can you please mark that with the letter M.

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG TRAPARA
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: So these were the lines, more or less; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG TRAPARA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we please save the map, and I would like to tender it in this form as a Defence exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be D276, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: When Dragomir Milosevic became the SRK commander, as you said, in August, what was the situation at that point in time in terms of combat and weaponry?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG TRAPARA
utterances.text: At that time when General Milosevic came, there was a truce at the lines and heavy weapons were withdrawn to 20 kilometres away from the town in the direction of Trnovo and Nisicka Visoravan.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: When it comes to your positions, can you describe those for us? Where did you spend your time?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG TRAPARA
utterances.text: You mean the troops?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: While on military assignments.

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG TRAPARA
utterances.text: In trenches.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: What did you have in terms of weapons?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG TRAPARA
utterances.text: In terms of weapons, each soldier had his own personal arm, be it an automatic or a semi-automatic rifle, as well as some heavier pieces which belonged to us according to the military establishment. We had anti-aircraft machine-guns and two Brownings.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Were you in possession of those throughout the war?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG TRAPARA
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Which of those did you not have when Dragomir Milosevic was commander?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG TRAPARA
utterances.text: I apologise, I thought you were asking me something else. We also had a PAT of 20-millimetre calibre that we had to take away before General Milosevic assumed command of the corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Did you have any heavy artillery throughout the conflict at those positions?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG TRAPARA
utterances.text: My unit, my company, did not have a single heavy piece. It was an infantry company and the troops had only their own personal weapons, as well as those proscribed by the establishment, those I've already mentioned.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: You mentioned a piece, you mentioned its calibre, 12 point something.

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG TRAPARA
utterances.text: It's a Browning 12.7-millimetre which was allowed to stay once the heavy pieces had been pulled out. It did not fall in the category of weapons that were supposed to be extracted and taken out by some 20 kilometres.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Since you were on those positions, as you described them, on the slopes of Mojmilo, what did those clashes look like during the more active periods, since you mentioned that there was a lull as well? What about 1992 and 1993 when military activities were more intensive?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG TRAPARA
utterances.text: There was an exchange of fire from both sides. If you look at the place where the stadium is on the map, there were some 40-millimetre pieces from 1992 until 1994. These were Bofors pieces and a Praga. But once orders were issued, these were withdrawn.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: When you say that there was an exchange of infantry weapons fire, what did that look like?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG TRAPARA
utterances.text: In most cases when there was exchange of fire of that type, they tried to reach Lukavica in depth, as far as possible, in order to disrupt communication that existed on the Lukavica-Pale road. We had nothing else to do but to open fire upon their trenches, since they had a commanding view of our positions.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: As for Mojmilo hill, you said that they were at a higher altitude. Concerning those dominating features of Mojmilo, what did that look like from the other side?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG TRAPARA
utterances.text: From the other side, or on the other side, the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina could control all of Lukavica, all the way up to Toplik from their positions, as well as Dobrinja IV, the Stari Celovac [phoen] settlement, and all the way up to Nedzarici.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Your Honour, for approximately the last five questions and answers or so, I've been struggling to understand the relevancy of military versus military activities in the southern part of the city. This does not have to do with any allegations of firing on civilians or injury to civilians or terrorising of civilians. We're getting an interesting and detailed account of army-versus-army actions, but I submit that it's not relevant.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Tapuskovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I'm trying to work on our case, Defence case, which is uniquely our own. We are not asked to deal with some matters that the Prosecutor tried to prove. We are trying to prove the various aspects of our case. Therefore, I don't think the Prosecutor can keep going to their assertions and the things they tried to prove when it comes to these dominating features. We hope that we will be able to prove that those dominating elevations were in the hands of the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina. I believe that at this moment we are in possession of evidence that at least 80 per cent of those dominating elevations were in the hands of the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina and that they had control from those positions on both sides.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Take it a step further now. You must take it a step further. Yes, you're trying to show that the elevated positions were in the hands of the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina and therefore what? It's your case, that's conceded, but it still has to be relevant. It still has to be relevant. That's an overriding, overarching requirement for admissibility. So you must take it a little further. I could take further in terms of the case that I that seen you trying to build, but let me hear how you establish the relevance, having said that the dominant positions were in the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina. How does that relate to the indictment? Because you can't get away from that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Certainly, we cannot get away from the indictment, but we dispute much of it, particularly pertaining to the time Dragomir Milosevic was accused of. I wanted to mention the only adjudicated fact from a previous case and wanted to share with you something we deem very important. It is very important to deal with the intensity of combat activities, particularly those undertaken by the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina. It is Defence case that the SRK activities were merely a response to their activities, particularly in that period, and that it was not a campaign with the aim to attack civilians. The victims in the territory controlled by the SRK are a good indicator of the intensity of combat activities undertaken by the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: All right. So you see, Mr. Docherty, this is how he establishes the relevance; that your case is that the SRK targeted civilians. His case, his response, is that that's not so. Two armies were fighting each other, in particular the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina occupied the dominant positions of the hills and there was no intent on the part of the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina to target civilians. They were merely fighting another army. No intent on the part of the Republika Srpska, rather, I correct myself, to target civilians. They were merely fighting another army, and that's the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina. And in my view, that does establish the relevance of the evidence. What the Chamber makes of it is another matter. But I would say that it is -- it's relevant.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, if I may, I would like to offer a couple of other things so as not to have to go back to this issue over and over again. It is very important, when it comes to adjudicated facts, I would like you to have a look at number 53, that is the adjudicated fact we accepted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Number 53, what is that one? I don't have the facts here.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, this is what it states: "In 1993, some 75.000 troops of the 1st Corps of the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina were deployed along the separation lines around Sarajevo. Some half of them were in the city itself, while the other half was on the separation lines outside the city." This fact had been made part of the case and we did not try to dispute that. It is a very good illustration of the circumstances and the nature of the situation, and it keeps pointing to the facts that we've tried to focus on during our case. We will dispute some other -- many other adjudicated facts and we will certainly be allowed to do so in view of the Appeals Chamber's decision, but the situation was one of a mix-up. We don't know who encircled whom, particularly since half of those 75.000 troops were inside Sarajevo, whereas the other half was around it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I believe you're speaking about the Appeals Chamber's decision in the adjudicated facts motion. We haven't actually read it yet. It was shown to me this morning, but I haven't actually read it. So you have an advantage over us, Mr. Tapuskovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. We've read it, but I was trying to point to the one that is already in existence. This was the one fact that we consented to, the adjudicated fact number 53. It is no longer in dispute. And it illustrates very well what the importance is of the matters we are trying to deal with in our case. What was important was the intensity of combat activities, particularly on the part of ABiH and particularly during the time of Dragomir Milosevic's command.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: But you need to go further, don't you, than just to show the intensity of the combat activities? I mean, bearing in mind that there's no burden on you to do anything at all, but to the extent that you're trying to rebut the Prosecution's case.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I understand that. In my view, one of the most important things is to rebut a thesis of the Prosecutor dealt with in paragraph 7. The entire first instance judgement in the Galic case is based on that argument in paragraph 7 as to when the hostilities broke out and who held the hills under their control.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, I will try to move at a greater pace now, but first can you tell me this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Tapuskovic, we'll take the break now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I should have said that in the absence of Judge Mindua, today's sitting takes place pursuant to the provisions of Rule 15 bis. Let the witness be brought in.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Please continue, Mr. Tapuskovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, can you tell me, in this time period preceding the arrival of the person who became head of the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps, what happened to soldiers and civilians? Were there any consequences?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG TRAPARA
utterances.text: Yes. They -- the BH army, after the end of 1994 and in early 1995 --

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: I'm asking you about the time before August 1994. In the course of those combat activities, were there any bad consequences for civilians and soldiers?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG TRAPARA
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, there were. In February 1994, my mother was wounded in front of our house. She was wounded from a rifle and both her bones beneath her knees were broken, and she's using crutches to this very day. There were many wounded civilians, especially on the Lukavica-Vrace road.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And now the time came when General Dragomir Milosevic became the head of the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps, and what did it look like then?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG TRAPARA
utterances.text: As I said before, when General Milosevic became commander of the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps, there was a truce, but one could sense that the BH army was preparing for combat operations, especially after the beginning of 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Until when was it quiet? Did anything happen in late 1994?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG TRAPARA
utterances.text: Yes, there was some fighting. There was some combat activity by the BH army.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Where?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG TRAPARA
utterances.text: Well, at the separation line between my company and ...

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And outside the lines where you were, did you know of any fighting?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG TRAPARA
utterances.text: Well, specifically at the lines held by my company and the neighbouring companies, there was sporadic firing but the large-scale combat took place towards Trnovo and the plateau there.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: At your lines there was sporadic firing. And how long did this go on, where you were?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG TRAPARA
utterances.text: Well, it went on like this until May 1995. In May the BH army became more active. They started firing more intensively at our lines and this culminated on the 16th of June.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And how come you remember this date, the 16th of June, as the culmination?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG TRAPARA
utterances.text: Well, I can't forget that date because my father was wounded by an enemy shell near Djukic Potok, below Mojmilo, and he lost a leg, he lost his liver, and then he died of his wounds.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Did anything else happen on that day?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG TRAPARA
utterances.text: On that same day, at position number 2 where the UN check-point was between the two sides, at 4.15 in the morning, the forces of the BH army took some UNPROFOR soldiers prisoner and they made an incursion behind our lines and killed eight soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: On the days that followed, do you remember any other events which stick in your memory?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG TRAPARA
utterances.text: Well, hardly had that fighting died down on the 16th of June, when towards the end of the month, from the area of Comagina's Kuca or Comagina's house, they fired from a sniper at the road and they threw hand grenades on our trenches.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Or rather, interpreter's correction: From hand-held launchers on our trenches.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: You mentioned --

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG TRAPARA
utterances.text: Comagina's Kuca or Comagina's house.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: I'll show you a document and please tell me does it have anything to do with what you just said.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's D107, a Defence exhibit. Can it please be shown to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Trapara, please read the heading slowly and what it says underneath the heading and the first paragraph.

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG TRAPARA
utterances.text: "Command of the 12th Division, strictly confidential number 02/2-7-10, Sarajevo, the 26th of June, 1995. Proposal of targets chosen to be destroyed, to tie up the aggressor forces, by unit. To the command of the 1st Corps."

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And now the first paragraph? Read it, please.

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG TRAPARA
utterances.text: The first or the second? "Pursuant to the order of the Chief of Staff of the 1st Corps, strictly confidential number 01/3-151 of the 25th of June, 1995. To carry out active combat operations in the area of responsibility of all brigades in the area of responsibility of the 12th Army Division in order to tie up the aggressor forces around the city and stretching them out, thus relieving our forces outside the city in the area of responsibility of the 14th and 16th Army Division, we send you proposals brigade by brigade."

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And now, just underneath this passage, you mentioned a place called Comagina's house. Read where it says "2 bb" and "3 bb".

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG TRAPARA
utterances.text: "2 bb in its zone of responsibility, a bunker in the house east of K, elevation point 648, 150 metres from the north, a group of six soldiers or fighters, a rifle, an M-53 light machine-gun, a sniper rifle, an automatic rifle. A dug-out south of Comagina Kuca, a group, an explosive device, four automatic rifles and a sniper rifle."

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Now, tell me, you mentioned Comagina Kuca, so please tell us what it says here. Does it correspond to what you have just been saying? And did you participate in this? And can you describe to Their Honours what this looked like.

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG TRAPARA
utterances.text: Yes. That's the position I just mentioned. I personally participated in this event. They attacked our bunker, our dug-out, below Comagina Kuca, firing from snipers and an explosive device.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And what happened?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG TRAPARA
utterances.text: We returned fire and very soon we pushed back that group to their starting position.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, look where it says "3 bb" right below that.

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG TRAPARA
utterances.text: "3 bb," or mountain battalion, "the sleeping quarters Cavarkapa Kuca, the Kaparuni RB RPG squad, a sniper rifle, a light machine-gun, an M-72, and AP with an attachment for a rifle launcher. The bunker near Comagina kuca, RO2/3bb a group of five fighters, a hand-held launcher, a sniper, an automatic rifle, an automatic rifle with an attachment for a rifle launcher."

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Did you have anything to do with this event?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG TRAPARA
utterances.text: Yes. I participated in this event also. This was some four or five hours after the first event.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us whether you remember anything about these events? Were there any casualties?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG TRAPARA
utterances.text: There were no casualties on our side. Later on I learnt that this had been a kind of simultaneous attack to get as many of our men as possible up on the lines in order, probably, to allow the other side to get most of their forces through the tunnel and into the Trnovo area.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: It says in the record that this was a simultaneous attack. Maybe you wanted to use another word. Do you know what the word "simultaneous" means?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG TRAPARA
utterances.text: Well, maybe I didn't express myself well. It was a real attack, but most probably it was meant to distract our attention.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: I don't want to lead. Well, you've explained what you meant. Do you remember anything else? Do you remember something being written on a wall?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG TRAPARA
utterances.text: I forgot to mention this just a while ago, but I do remember this: It was on the 16th of June when we got back our line at 2030 hours in the evening. It said on Rajko Lalovic's house, "Greetings from Zenica."

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And how did you interpret this message?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG TRAPARA
utterances.text: Well, we interpreted it to mean that there had been a special unit from Zenica there which attacked that part of our unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell Their Honours how long the offensive lasted and whether there were any casualties among the soldiers and the civilians?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG TRAPARA
utterances.text: Yes. The offensive lasted, and on that day there were casualties. That day over 150 shells dropped. There were casualties among the soldiers; about ten civilians were killed and there were some children who had their legs blown off in Lukavica, in the depth. They probably fired into the depth at Lukavica in order to prevent reinforcements to reach the front lines.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I have no further questions. Witness, thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Docherty.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Good morning, sir. My name is John Docherty. I'm one of the Prosecutors on this side of the courtroom and I'll be asking you a few questions this morning. If you have any difficulty understanding my questions, please ask me to clear it up and I'll be happy to do that before we move on. Is that all right?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG TRAPARA
utterances.text: Yes, that's all right.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: To begin with, were you a company commander throughout the war or is that a position that you were promoted to during the war?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG TRAPARA
utterances.text: I was a company commander throughout the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: And while Mr. Tapuskovic was asking you questions, you testified about who your battalion commander was and who your brigade commander was. If I use the term "chain of command," do you have an understanding of what I mean?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG TRAPARA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: A chain of command means that more senior officers give orders to less senior officers give orders to junior officers, and so on, and it is a way, one way, by which a senior commander can stay truly in command of a military formation. Would you agree with what I've just said?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG TRAPARA
utterances.text: Yes, it is one of the ways, but it doesn't always have to be that way.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Of course. And that leads, actually, to my next question. During the time that you were an office -- that you were serving with the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps, that corps had a functioning chain of command, did it not? The brigade commander gave orders to the battalion commander gave orders to you, and so on; correct?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG TRAPARA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: And it was your understanding that this chain of command went right to the very top and that it was first General Galic and then General Milosevic who was in control of the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps.

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG TRAPARA
utterances.text: That's probably how it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Was there any doubt in your mind that during the time that he was in command, August of 1994 onwards, that General Milosevic was truly the commander of the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps and could give orders to the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps with the expectation that they would be obeyed?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG TRAPARA
utterances.text: I personally had no doubt.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: One other thing that you testified about was the sorts of weapons that your company had, and before I move on, just one other background question. As a company commander, what rank did you hold in the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG TRAPARA
utterances.text: I was a captain.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: And as a captain, you were a commissioned officer.

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG TRAPARA
utterances.text: I was a reserve officer.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: And how many men were in your company? I understand that probably fluctuated, but on average how -- I just want to get a sense how big a unit this was that you commanded.

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG TRAPARA
utterances.text: It ranged from 180 to 130 men. The average was 150.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: And how many platoons were in this company?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG TRAPARA
utterances.text: Four.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: You testified earlier about the types of weapons that you had in this company and you said that there were no heavy weapons possessed by your company. I want to broaden that a little bit. As a company commander, could you call on heavy weapons for support of operations that your company was engaged in?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG TRAPARA
utterances.text: I could call, I personally, as a commander, just the mortars that were actually under the authority of the battalion.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: What was the size of the mortars that were under the command of the battalion? Were these 82s, were these 120s, a mix of those sorts? Can you tell us that?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG TRAPARA
utterances.text: 82 millimetres.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: How many 82-millimetre mortars did the battalion have? And to the best of your recollection, whereabouts were they located?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG TRAPARA
utterances.text: It had three 82-millimetre mortars.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: And whereabouts were they in relation to your company's area of responsibility?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG TRAPARA
utterances.text: If we looked from the -- if you looked from my company towards the internal part, then it was sort of to the south, southwest. I can actually give you the name of the place where we were.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Can you give us the place of -- sorry, the name of the place where the mortars were?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG TRAPARA
utterances.text: The name was Prljavo Brdo.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: I don't, I'm sorry to say, speak your language, but "brdo" typically means hill. Was this an elevated position where the mortars were?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG TRAPARA
utterances.text: It wasn't that much of an elevation. It was in the depth of the territory away from the front lines at an elevation. That's where the mortars were. It's not a big elevation. It's a sort of low-lying area. The name was Prljavo Brdo, but it wasn't really a proper hill.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: All right. We'll come back to the hills in a couple of minutes, but I have a few more questions about weaponry before we do that. You testified on direct examination that heavy weapons were to be taken 20 kilometres away. Do you remember this conversation with Mr. Tapuskovic?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG TRAPARA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: And do you remember saying that, for example, the Browning that was in your company was allowed to be kept because its 12.7-millimetre calibre meant that it was not a heavy weapon and did not need to be moved out. Do you remember saying that.

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG TRAPARA
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: If we could please see Prosecution Exhibit 667 on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Mr. Trapara, what I'm -- what is going to come up on the screen, I'll just tell you while we're waiting for it to load, is an order from Dragomir Milosevic and it deals with the subject of heavy weapons and the exclusion zone for heavy weapons. I'm going to ask -- my first question, when it comes up, will be whether you have seen this document, whether you are familiar with it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. -- Please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Do you see, Witness, that this is dated the 21st of August, 1994? It's in the upper left. Is that the date of the document?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG TRAPARA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: And do you remember testifying, when Mr. Tapuskovic was examining you, that shortly after Dragomir Milosevic took command, the heavy weapons had to be taken away? Do you remember relating those two events: Dragomir Milosevic takes command; shortly afterwards, the heavy weapons are taken 20 kilometres away. Do you remember that testimony, sir?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG TRAPARA
utterances.text: I said that the weapons were pulled back upon the arrival of General Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. And General Milosevic took command around the middle of August of 1994. I believe the exact date was the 12th, but the middle of August. Is that something you and I can agree on?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG TRAPARA
utterances.text: I really don't know the exact date.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Can we agree that it was approximately the middle of August of 1994?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG TRAPARA
utterances.text: It's hard to answer this question. I don't know the precise date, so it would be difficult for me to respond to this question. I know that it was in August, but ...

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: That's close enough.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: And could we please scroll down on the B/C/S side so that the witness can see the signature on this document, and it might mean going to page 2.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Now, there is a name at the bottom there; correct? And the name is Dragomir Milosevic; is that right?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG TRAPARA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: And it's not signed, but this is a telex and most military telexes are not signed; is that also correct? Just a printed name.

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG TRAPARA
utterances.text: Yes, I see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: All right. Now, I want to direct your attention to paragraph number 3 because you testified that these heavy weapons were withdrawn. Do you see paragraph number 3 down towards the bottom of the page?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG TRAPARA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: All right. Does that paragraph say that heavy weapons within the 20-kilometre zone are to be camouflaged?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG TRAPARA
utterances.text: That's what it says in this paper.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Does it say they are to be hidden?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG TRAPARA
utterances.text: That's what it says.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Does it say they are to be moved only at night?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG TRAPARA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: And does it say that all police and other security measures are to be taken so that any movements of these weapons will be concealed from UNPROFOR?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG TRAPARA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Is this the 20-kilometre pull-back of heavy weapons that you were testifying about in your direct examination, Mr. Trapara?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG TRAPARA
utterances.text: During the examination-in-chief, I talked about what I know and what I heard. As for the heavy weapons, as far as my unit is concerned.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter is not quite sure what the witness said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Witness, will you please repeat what you just said?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I haven't seen this document or heard about it before, but I did respect the order, I myself, as the company commander. What I said during the examination-in-chief, I abide by, that the weapons were pulled back 20 kilometres from the town.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: And you have also testified, not once now but several times, that you were in a unit that did not itself have heavy weapons; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG TRAPARA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Now I want to move on to the subject we touched on just a moment -- a couple of minutes ago and that has to do with the hills. You mentioned several hills in your direct testimony, and after you mentioned these hills you said that the dominating positions on these hills were occupied by the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina; Zuc and Hum, Debelo Brdo, some others as well. Were you aware before you came here to testify that the fact that Zuc and Hum and Debelo Brdo were occupied by the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina was evidence put in during the Prosecution's case months ago? Did you know that before you testified?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG TRAPARA
utterances.text: I knew that Zuc hill was captured and Hum always was under the control of the B and H army. When I testified about that, I talked about the period when General Milosevic became the corps commander, about the situation that was in force then at the time regarding the hills and the elevations. But I know that Zuc was captured earlier by the B and H army.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Are you also aware that each of these hills that you testified about can be looked down upon from the heights of other hills, and even mountains in some cases, that were under the control of the army of Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG TRAPARA
utterances.text: I'm not aware that you could overlook them. It all depends on the situation, where you are looking from. Perhaps they can be overlooked but you cannot fire, you cannot fire beyond those hills if the objective was to fire at civilians.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Let's take an example to illustrate the point.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Could we please see 65 ter number 03211.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: And this, Mr. Trapara, while we're waiting for it to load, is going to be a map. I'm going to ask the registrar to zoom in on an area on the southern central part of the map which is the elevation called Debelo Brdo. As a former infantry officer, I take it that you can read a relief map quite easily; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG TRAPARA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: And I'm also going to ask the usher to assist you, and what I want you to do is, on this map, locate Debelo Brdo and then just draw a circle around that feature. And when you draw the circle, please don't obscure any information about the height in metres of the hill because I'm going to ask you about that, okay? So draw the circle without going through the height.

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG TRAPARA
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Okay. And just above the point -- the red circle that you made, do you see the height 745 in metres?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG TRAPARA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Now, you testified that since you were in the Scouts, you've been tramping through the hills around Sarajevo; in fact, you've lived in Lukavica all your life. Would you agree, even if you don't know it to the metre, Debelo Brdo is about 745 metres high?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG TRAPARA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Now, a little bit to the south of Debelo Brdo we see a hill called Grad. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG TRAPARA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: And the height listed for Grad is 823 metres; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG TRAPARA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: And if we go to the lower right-hand portion of the screen, we see a height, and the name is not entirely on the screen, but do you see the height 1.080 metres?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG TRAPARA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: And so this is what I mean by the point that Debelo Brdo was overlooked by other hills from which you could look down on it. Would you agree with me that these higher elevations are under the control -- during the armed conflict, were under the control of the army of Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG TRAPARA
utterances.text: Yes, they were under the control -- well, the territory was held by he army Republika Srpska. But this very peak of 1.080 metres was impossible to use for direct fire. If you look at this ridge that goes from the peak, that is, 1.080, to the town, it's flat so there's no theoretical chance of any firing from that spot at the town. I know that area; I know what it looks like. It's impossible to fire from this elevation 1.080 at the town.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: The point I'm making is a more general point, Mr. Trapara. Sarajevo sits in the valley of the Miljacka River; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG TRAPARA
utterances.text: A part of Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: And it is ringed by high hills; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG TRAPARA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: And yes, some of the inner hills, the ones closer to the city, were held by the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina, but as you go back further away from town, you get to hills that were held by the army of Republika Srpska; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG TRAPARA
utterances.text: To the depth of the territory, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: And those hills under the control of the army of Republika Srpska were higher than the ones controlled by the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina, generally speaking?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG TRAPARA
utterances.text: They are higher if you look at the actual elevation, but they were not positioned in such a way, like the ones that I referred to.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Excuse me. You also indicated in your direct testimony, and there was quite a bit of --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Docherty, he should explain what he means when he says that they are concededly higher "but not positioned in such a way, like the ones that I referred to." What do you mean by that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, what I meant was, I was thinking of elevation 1.080. It is higher than the Debelo Brdo elevation, but from this elevation there is a flat area going towards the town, so it's impossible to fire at the town from that elevation, the 1.080 metres elevation.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Well, let's turn from the 1.080 metres elevation to the hill of Grad. If you walk off the top of Debelo Brdo going south, you can see on this map that first you go down and then you start coming back up towards Grad. Am I right so far?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG TRAPARA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: And when you're up on top of Grad, you are looking down on the top of Debelo Brdo, aren't you?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG TRAPARA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: And as an experienced infantry officer, how enthusiastic would you be about occupying the top of Debelo Brdo if the enemy was 80 metres above you on a hill a short distance away? Is that something you would lead your men into?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG TRAPARA
utterances.text: It all depends on the view from one hill and the other hill. It depended on what would the view be from Debelo Brdo and from the other hill. But I'm not quite sure what it says here. I'm not sure whether this was in the area of responsibility of the army of Republika Srpska because the lines were right below the road. This place, Grad, has no purpose here. This red line is the main road going towards the -- towards Pale. There is a bend in the road from Miljevici. These were old trenches; they were lined with sacks of sand. So I don't really see the point of Grad here at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: I'd like to move on, but let me -- two things: Number one, you may not know this, but there has been evidence in this case from a Defence witness who was shown photographs of this area, and we can rely upon that if you, yourself, are not entirely familiar with where things are. And secondly, when you were asked by Mr. Tapuskovic to talk about hills that were under the control of the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina, you did not yourself mention Grad at that time, did you?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG TRAPARA
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: The next topic that I want to turn to is the question of the intensity --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Tapuskovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, speaking of the Grad elevation, the witness said that he doesn't know under whose control it was. He already said that he didn't know in which area of responsibility it was. The one -- the 893 elevation, he said that he didn't know whether there was the army of Republika Srpska there, or anyone, for that matter. He expressed his doubt as to whether that particular elevation was under the control of the army of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: That is a correct recapitulation of what the witness testified to, Your Honour, and that's why I moved on. And, for the record, the reference I made to another witness was to the evidence of Mr. Milorad Katic, who, in cross-examination, was shown a photograph taken from Grad down towards Debelo Brdo, and stated that the photograph had been taken from positions of the army of Republika Srpska. So I thought that since this witness said he wasn't sure, the better thing was to move on and let the evidence show --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: But you didn't actually put that to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: I simply gave it to the witness as an explanation of why I was moving on. It wasn't in the form of a question. You are correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Docherty.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Am I free to move on?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Okay, thank you. I'll tender this map, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, we admit it. Mr. Docherty, what was concerning me was the -- was how proper it was for you not to have put to the witness what the previous witness said, but yet you narrated it to us, so that it would influence -- it could influence the subsequent evidence of a witness without you having put it to him. In my view, it would have been more proper for you to have put it to the witness, if you intend to rely on it.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: I assure you I meant nothing improper. I was simply trying to let -- not keep the witness in the dark as to where he was being led. But once the map is finished with being put in, I can certainly put the question to the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: And will.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be Exhibit P791, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Mr. Trapara, I put it to you that Grad hill was under the control of the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina. Do you agree or do you disagree with that? I'm sorry, the army -- the ABiH, if I didn't say that. I'm sorry, I've completely -- I'm sorry, no, that's entirely my mistake. I apologise. I withdraw that question. I meant to ask this question: Mr. Trapara, I put it to you that Grad hill was under the control of the army of Republika Srpska. Do you agree with me, do you disagree with me, or do you not know?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG TRAPARA
utterances.text: I do not know. I'm uncertain. I'm more inclined to disagree with you, but I am not certain. As for the Grad 893 elevation, I'm confused by this road just below, because that's where the ABiH lines were.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: I want to talk with you for a couple of minutes about intensity of fighting. When you were in your examination-in-chief, you testified about the intensity of fighting. And are you aware, and again I'm going to make reference to other evidence in this case, that the Prosecution has introduced a report from a statistician and that report indicates that civilians died at a rate, at a frequency, that had nothing whatever to do with the intensity of combat operations? So my first question is: Are you aware of this evidence?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG TRAPARA
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: And my second --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Tapuskovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Since we are discussing the intensity, could we have a temporal reference? If we have the indictment here pertaining to one period of time, then perhaps the Prosecutor should tell us which period exactly he has in mind when discussing intensity.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Docherty.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: 1992 through and including 1995, both the Galic and the Milosevic time periods.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: And you've indicated, am I correct, Witness, you're not aware of this evidence?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG TRAPARA
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: During the time that you were a company commander with the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps, were you aware of allegations, whether made by human rights organisations, reported in the international press, or from any other source, that the army of Republika Srpska was committing atrocities and war crimes against civilians? Were you aware of those allegations?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG TRAPARA
utterances.text: I only listened to the federal news or the Sarajevo television news and I'm not aware of such allegations.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Are you aware of any investigations, inquiries, administrative proceedings, within the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps into allegations that troops of the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps have committed such crimes?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Tapuskovic. Don't answer. Mr. Tapuskovic has a point.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I would understand if the witness were asked whether he committed an atrocity or a crime or if he has any knowledge of such incidents. But to ask him whether he heard of any NGO reports or any other reports which are second- or third-hand, that is inappropriate, in my view. In my view, he should be asked about the things he knows as to whether such things, indeed, happened and what is his direct knowledge of them. Also, he could be asked whether he ever received any such orders to commit atrocities. But to ask him things he was supposed to learn from other people, well, I don't think that is proper.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: But if you were in my jurisdiction, my domestic jurisdiction, yes. But it's well known that here we receive hearsay evidence. Well, let him say whether he knows or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Do you remember the question?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG TRAPARA
utterances.text: I do, and I answered already. I followed the media, the Sarajevo or the federation television, but I had no occasion to hear of such things.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: And then the follow-up question to that one was whether you are aware from any source of any military prosecutions, administrative discipline, inquiries, investigations into allegations that troops of the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps had committed war crimes and atrocities. Are you aware of any such proceedings?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG TRAPARA
utterances.text: In what time? Could you please explain.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: August 12th of 1994 until the Dayton Agreements.

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG TRAPARA
utterances.text: I am not aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: The last topic that I want to cover with you, Mr. Trapara, concerns the incident on October the 15th of 1991 that Mr. Tapuskovic began his direct examination with. On October the 15th of 1991, at about 2.00 in the morning, you were in a truck; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG TRAPARA
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: At this point could we please see ter number 3342, but could it not be broadcast, as it contains information that was withheld by going into private session.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: And, Mr. Trapara, the document that is coming up, I am going to be careful not to mention any of the names in the document and I would ask you to do the same when you're asking the questions. Is that agreeable?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG TRAPARA
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: And this, you will see, is a report prepared by the MUP.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: And I'll ask if we could please look at page 2 of both the English and the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: And it was your testimony on direct that you knew nothing of the contents of that truck that you were in at 2.00 in the morning on the 15th of October, 1991. Is that your evidence, sir?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG TRAPARA
utterances.text: Until we arrived at our destination in the village of Ivanovici.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: And you see that this is a report concerning the police stop of that truck, don't you?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG TRAPARA
utterances.text: I do see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: And you see that the police indicate that they stopped the trucks -- they stopped the truck, excuse me, "managed in a repeated attempt to stop a truck (the truck did not stop at the first warning of the militia patrol)." Do you see the part that I've just read?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG TRAPARA
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: The truck driver tried to get away. Isn't that what's being said here?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG TRAPARA
utterances.text: That's what it reads.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: All right. Well, it also reads that once the truck was stopped, you and another individual ran away; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG TRAPARA
utterances.text: That's what it reads.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: And when you told Mr. Tapuskovic in direct examination that you went back to your work at the post office the next day, that's because you had run away from the police the night before, not because the police had decided not to take you into custody; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG TRAPARA
utterances.text: On the spot when the truck stopped, within ten minutes two police vehicles arrived. The policemen came out of their vehicles asking who the driver of the truck was. The driver said, "I am." Then he was asked to climb into the truck and start the engine. And another policeman entered the passenger cabin with him. They went towards Vrace.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: I have to stop you. The question I asked was that you ran away and that's why you were not taken into custody at 2.00 in the morning. And can you tell us if that's correct or not correct? You ran away and the police didn't catch you that night.

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG TRAPARA
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Okay. They caught you later that night?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG TRAPARA
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: You did run away; correct?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG TRAPARA
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: This is what it says in the report, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG TRAPARA
utterances.text: This is an incorrect report. As I said, they only asked about the driver. They made him climb into the truck and left for Vrace. Out of the rest, the seven of us, no one was taken away.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: All right. And --

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG TRAPARA
utterances.text: And I state this in full responsibility.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: And this report was prepared by the MUP of, as you testified in your own direct examination, the MUP of the Federal Socialist Republic of Yugoslavia; correct? Because it's an October 15th, 1991 document; correct?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG TRAPARA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Not by any Bosnian organisation but by a federal Yugoslavian organisation; correct?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG TRAPARA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Now, if we could scroll down in the English a little more, I want to take a look at what was in this truck.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: And I'm just going to read: "The following items were found in the truck." I'll ask you to find it in the B/C/S version and make sure that I read it properly. "Two hand-held launchers; two optical sights in original boxes; two stands for hand-held launchers; two cleaning devices for hand-held launchers; four wooden cases containing 40 semi-automatic rifles with accompanying technical specifications; ammunition pouches and cleaning devices; seven semi-automatic rifles; four wooden cases containing 3.600 7.9-millimetre bullets; eight wooden cases containing 8.960 7.62-millimetre bullets; one case containing two heavy machine-guns, M-53, with accompanying equipment, technical specifications and cleaning accessories." Is that what I have read, sir? Have I read that correctly?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG TRAPARA
utterances.text: You have.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: And it is your testimony that you got into this truck, making this trip at 2.00 in the morning, containing quite a little collection of armaments, but had no idea yourself of what was in the truck.

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG TRAPARA
utterances.text: I had no knowledge of what was on the truck until the place it was stopped. Until it stopped, I had no knowledge of its contents.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: You were simply asked to get in this truck at 2.00 in the morning and in you went. Is that your testimony?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG TRAPARA
utterances.text: The driver asked me to.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Isn't it actually correct, sir, that even as far back as October 15th of 1991, you were involved in Bosnian Serb nationalist activities of the most extreme sort, and that's why you were in that truck that night, delivering this load of fire-power?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG TRAPARA
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Are you aware of the speech that Dr. Radovan Karadzic gave to the Bosnian Serb Assembly on the night this truck was stopped in which he said that the Muslim people of Bosnia and Herzegovina faced, his word, "disappearance"? Have you heard that speech? Have you heard of that speech?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG TRAPARA
utterances.text: I didn't follow the speech, but I have heard of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: And that speech was given either the day that -- well, it was 2.00 in the morning, so the day before the truck was stopped; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG TRAPARA
utterances.text: I wouldn't know when he gave the speech. I cannot remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: And haven't your political sympathies, which I characterised a couple of questions ago as extremist, continued right down to this day? Are those still the views that you held -- that you hold, I mean?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG TRAPARA
utterances.text: Please explain. It is unclear to me. What political sympathies?

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: What I'm putting to you, sir, is the following: That this stop of the truck full of guns was an out-growth of your involvement in extremist and violent politics. And I put it to you that those political sympathies, those viewpoints, are colouring and shaping the testimony that you give to this Court. In other words, I'm saying that you have an interest in the outcome of this case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, you have asked several questions and I think they should be separated. The first question being put to you, Witness, is that the truck in which you were and which was full of guns was an out-growth of your involvement in extremist and violent politics. Do you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: It is also being put to you that those political sympathies, those viewpoints, influence the testimony that you're giving today.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] At the time I did not belong to any political party, neither at that time nor during the war.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: I have no more questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Any re-examination, Mr. Tapuskovic?
